title: Japanese American Buddhists and Buddhism Today
bigQuestion: How have Buddhist communities in America kept, changed and shared their traditions?

story.title: From a Barracks to a Temple
story.kicker: A priest leads services in a camp barracks, and years later his community has a temple in Chicago.
paragraphs: In 1942, after Japan attacked Pearl Harbor, the U.S. government forced about 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry on the West Coast into inland camps. Most were U.S. citizens. Many were members of Jodo Shinshu Buddhist temples.

In the camps, people lived in rows of tar-paper barracks. Buddhist priests held services in whatever rooms they could find. Families chanted, listened to Dharma talks and kept Obon and the Buddha's birthday, even behind barbed wire.

Some Buddhists were watched with special suspicion, and some priests were held apart from their families. Still, the communities held together. Young people ran Sunday schools. Older members led chanting when no priest was near.

When families were allowed to leave, many moved to Chicago for work. In 1944, two new Buddhist temples began in the city: the Buddhist Temple of Chicago and the Midwest Buddhist Temple. Both still serve their communities today.
story.think: What helped these Buddhist communities hold together in the camps?

lessons.title: Buddhist Churches of America
lessons.mainIdea: Japanese immigrants brought Jodo Shinshu to America, and their organization took the name Buddhist Churches of America in 1944.
reading: Japanese immigrants began arriving in Hawaii and on the West Coast in the late 1800s. Many were Jodo Shinshu Buddhists. In 1899, two priests came to San Francisco and started what became the Buddhist Mission of North America.

Temples grew in California, Washington and Oregon. To fit American life, many used pews, hymnals, Sunday services and Sunday schools. Some called themselves 'Buddhist churches'. Services were often in English.

In 1944, while many members were still in the camps, the organization changed its name to the *Buddhist Churches of America* (BCA). Today it is one of the oldest Buddhist organizations in the United States. Scholars call such changes *adaptation*.

words.d: the national organization of Jodo Shinshu temples in the U.S., named in 1944
Shin Buddhism, a Japanese Pure Land tradition centered on Amida Buddha
changing to fit a new place or situation

lessons.title: Faith in the Camps
lessons.mainIdea: During the 1942–45 incarceration, Japanese American Buddhists kept their practice going under hard conditions.
reading: The camps were built in remote places like Manzanar in California, Heart Mountain in Wyoming and Topaz in Utah. Families lived in crowded barracks, with little privacy. There were ten main camps in all.

Buddhists faced extra suspicion because their religion was linked to Japan. Some priests were arrested early and held in separate camps. Still, Buddhist services, festivals and Sunday schools went on in the camps, often led by laypeople.

In 1988, the U.S. government formally apologized for the incarceration and paid *reparations* to survivors. Buddhist temples today keep the *memory* of the camps through services, exhibits and pilgrimages to the old camp sites.

words.d: payments made to make up for a wrong
what a community remembers and keeps alive about its past

lessons.title: Two Chicago Temples, 1944
lessons.mainIdea: In 1944, Japanese Americans leaving the camps founded the Buddhist Temple of Chicago and the Midwest Buddhist Temple.
reading: People leaving the camps could not return to the West Coast at first. Thousands moved to Chicago, where jobs were available. They started new lives in neighborhoods on the North and South Sides.

In 1944, Rev. Gyomay Kubose and others started what is now the *Buddhist Temple of Chicago*. The same year, another group founded the *Midwest Buddhist Temple*, which later built a temple in the Old Town neighborhood. Both are Jodo Shinshu temples.
The Midwest Buddhist Temple is known for its summer Ginza Holiday festival, with Japanese food, crafts and performances. Both temples offer services in English and welcome visitors.

words.d: a Shin Buddhist temple founded in Chicago in 1944 by Japanese Americans
a Shin Buddhist temple founded in Chicago in 1944, now in Old Town

lessons.title: Immigrant Temples After 1965
lessons.mainIdea: After the 1965 immigration law and the wars in Southeast Asia, many new Buddhist communities formed across America.
reading: The *Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965* ended quotas that had kept out most Asian immigrants. Families from Thailand, Sri Lanka, Korea, Taiwan, China and elsewhere began arriving in larger numbers.

After 1975, refugees from Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos resettled across the U.S., including in Illinois. They built temples in homes, storefronts and later large buildings. These temples help keep language, food and family customs alive.

Today many immigrant temples serve as community centers too. They hold language classes, festivals and youth groups. Scholars note that these communities make up a large share of American Buddhists, even though they appear less often in the media. They are part of the *diaspora*.

words.d: a U.S. law that ended national quotas and opened immigration from Asia
a community living far from its original homeland

lessons.title: Convert Communities and Meditation Centers
lessons.mainIdea: Since the 1950s, many Americans have joined Buddhism as converts, often through meditation centers.
reading: In the 1950s and 1960s, writers and students became interested in Zen, partly through D.T. Suzuki's books. Japanese teachers such as Shunryu Suzuki founded the San Francisco Zen Center in 1962. Tibetan teachers came after fleeing Tibet in 1959.

In the 1970s, Americans who had studied in Asia founded *meditation centers* in the Theravada vipassana, or insight, tradition. Many convert Buddhists focus on meditation, retreats and study more than on rituals or festivals.

Scholars sometimes talk of 'two Buddhisms' in America: immigrant temples and convert centers. Others say this split is too simple, since many communities mix both and the children of immigrants and converts share practices.

words.d: places where people gather to learn and practice meditation
insight meditation, a practice in the Theravada tradition

lessons.title: Public Teachers
lessons.mainIdea: The Dalai Lama and Thich Nhat Hanh became world-famous Buddhist teachers through books, talks and peace work.
reading: The *Dalai Lama*, Tenzin Gyatso (born 1935), is the 14th Dalai Lama, a leading figure of Tibetan Buddhism. He fled Tibet in 1959 and has lived in exile in India. He received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1989.

*Thich Nhat Hanh* (1926–2022) was a Vietnamese Zen monk. He worked for peace during the Vietnam War and was nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize by Martin Luther King Jr. in 1967. Exiled from Vietnam, he founded Plum Village in France.

Both wrote many books in English and spoke to large audiences. Their teachings on compassion, mindfulness and peace reached many people who are not Buddhist. Scholars note that their public images are one part of much larger traditions. The Dalai Lama leads in *exile*.

words.d: a leading teacher of Tibetan Buddhism; the 14th is Tenzin Gyatso (born 1935)
Vietnamese Zen monk and peace activist (1926–2022)

lessons.title: From Sati to Mindfulness
lessons.mainIdea: The English word 'mindfulness' translates the Pali sati, a practice described in the suttas.
reading: The Pali word *sati* means remembering or keeping in mind. T.W. Rhys Davids chose the English word 'mindfulness' for it in 1881, and the translation stuck. It appears in Buddhist verse and prose alike.

In the Pali Canon, sati is one step of the Eightfold Path, 'right mindfulness'. The Satipatthana Sutta (Majjhima Nikaya 10) describes four foundations of mindfulness: body, feelings, mind and mental objects.

In the suttas, mindfulness is part of a whole path that includes ethics, wisdom and the goal of nibbana. Scholars point out that modern uses of the word often focus on attention and calm and leave out that wider *context*.

words.d: the Pali word translated as mindfulness; remembering or keeping in mind
the setting that gives a word or idea its full meaning

lessons.title: Mindfulness Programs
lessons.mainIdea: Since 1979, secular mindfulness programs have spread in hospitals, schools and businesses.
reading: In 1979, Jon Kabat-Zinn started Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) at the University of Massachusetts Medical School. He drew on Buddhist meditation but taught it without religious language.

Programs like MBSR spread to hospitals, schools, sports teams and workplaces. Researchers have studied their effects on stress and attention. These programs describe themselves as *secular*, meaning not religious.

Some Buddhist teachers welcome this spread, saying it helps many people. Others worry that removing ethics and the larger Buddhist path changes the practice. Critics sometimes use the term 'McMindfulness' for programs sold only to boost productivity.

words.d: not religious; not connected to a religion
Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction, a program started by Jon Kabat-Zinn in 1979

lessons.title: Buddhism in America Today
lessons.mainIdea: American Buddhism today includes many traditions, communities and debates, from Chicago temples to meditation apps.
reading: Walk through Chicago today and you can find Shin temples from 1944, Thai and Sri Lankan temples, Vietnamese and Cambodian temples, Tibetan centers, Korean Seon temples and Zen groups. Each keeps its own *heritage*.

American Buddhists debate many questions: how to pass traditions to children, the role of women as teachers and nuns, how to include people of all backgrounds, and how to respond to the popularity of mindfulness.
From the 1893 Parliament to the temples of 1944 and the communities of today, Chicago has been part of this story. Scholars describe it as a history of both *continuity* and change.

words.d: traditions and customs handed down from the past
staying the same or connected over time
